overview: Downer EDI is one of Australia's and New Zealand's largest integrated infrastructure services providers, employing around 26,000 people across more than 500 sites. It designs, builds, operates and maintains essential infrastructure — roads, rail, power, gas, water, telecommunications, and government/defence facilities — for public and private sector customers, largely under long-term outsourcing contracts. The company has spent the past three years executing a turnaround: exiting non-core and underperforming businesses, resetting risk guardrails on contract bidding, and driving margin recovery after a 2023 earnings restatement and impairment crisis.

business_model.summary: Downer earns revenue from long-dated, largely non-discretionary maintenance and outsourcing contracts (recurring, annuity-like) alongside project/construction work (episodic, lower visibility) across three segments: Transport, Energy & Utilities, and Facilities. Growth in profitability since FY23 has come mainly from margin recovery (disciplined tendering, cost-out, exit of loss-making legacy contracts) rather than revenue growth, with pro forma revenue actually declining as the company prunes its portfolio and applies tighter risk guardrails.

revenue_streams.name: Transport (roads, rail & transit systems, NZ projects/Hawkins)
Energy & Utilities (power, gas, water, telco, industrial & energy)
Facilities (government, health, education, defence outsourcing)
revenue_streams.trend: stable revenue, resilient margin, defence contract ramp-up pressure near term

business_model.customer_type: B2B/B2G — predominantly government and government-adjacent customers (defence, transport agencies, utilities, education, health) plus large private infrastructure owners (e.g., AusNet, Chorus, Powerco, Transgrid, nbn); revenue is contract-based with multi-year terms rather than transactional
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia and New Zealand only; no material international exposure

competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest diversified infrastructure services companies in Australia/NZ; no single competitor matches Downer's breadth across transport, energy & utilities, and facilities, though it faces focused specialists in each vertical (Ventia in government/telco outsourcing, Fulton Hogan in roading, UGL/John Holland in transport and power projects)

moat_factors.factor: Scale and breadth of integrated capability
moat_factors.description: 26,000 employees, 500+ sites, and end-to-end capability across multiple infrastructure verticals is difficult for narrower rivals to replicate, supporting bundled/large program wins (e.g., $38.5bn work-in-hand at FY26)

moat_factors.factor: Incumbency and switching costs on long-dated contracts
moat_factors.description: Multi-year field services and asset management agreements (e.g., Chorus 7-year $500m, Powerco 12-year $540m, AusNet gas extension) create embedded relationships and re-tender advantages, though contracts are periodically re-tendered competitively

Long track record as a prime contractor for Defence, state transport agencies and utilities; named 2025 Australian Prime Contractor of the Year, but this is offset by reputational damage from the 2023 restatement and ongoing ACCC cartel allegations
Owns bitumen/asphalt manufacturing and rollingstock design/build/maintenance capability, giving some cost and technical advantages in Road Services and Rail & Transit Systems

weaknesses: Structurally thin margins typical of services/construction contracting (targeting only ~5-6% EBITA margin by FY30) leave little room for cost overruns or contract mispricing
History of contract mispricing and revenue misreporting (2022-23 utilities contract scandal, $539.5m FY23 impairment) shows weak historical risk controls, now being rebuilt
Reliant on public-sector budgets and tendering cycles which are subject to political and fiscal cycle risk
Ongoing legal overhang: consolidated shareholder class action (Vic Supreme Court, since 2023) and ACCC cartel/price-fixing proceedings (Dec 2024) against subsidiary Spotless

growth_drivers: Energy transition investment (transmission, substations, renewables connection, gas network maintenance) driving Energy & Utilities demand — a stated 'above cycle growth' target for Power and Water
Defence capability build-out — new Facilities and infrastructure contracts with Australian and NZ Defence (e.g., $220m CASG agreement, EMOS extension)
Population growth and government services infrastructure (health, education, housing) supporting Facilities segment

Large multi-year transport programs — Queensland Train Manufacturing Program, Auckland City Rail Link, Auckland Airport Domestic Jet Terminal, Ōtaki to North of Levin highway — underpinning a record $38.5bn work-in-hand (+10% YoY) at FY26
Continued cost-out program ($213m achieved cumulative to FY25, exceeding upsized $200m target) and further margin uplift toward a ~6% EBITA margin FY30 target

Capital allocation shift to shareholder returns — buyback restarted H1 FY26 ($64.4m; ~$96.5m of a ~$260m program completed by FY26) and dividend growth (29.2cps FY26, +31% CAGR over three years) now that balance sheet is repaired (net debt/EBITDA 0.8x FY26, BBB Fitch rating)

business.description: Downer's business model depends on accurately pricing and executing large, long-dated contracts; the FY23 crisis (loss-making utilities contract misreported since FY20, $539.5m impairment, -$385.7m net loss) shows the consequences when this fails; risk guardrails are new and unproven through a full cycle

Pro forma revenue has fallen in FY24, FY25 and FY26 as the company exits non-core/underperforming contracts; management is betting margin gains outpace the shrinking base, but the strategy leaves limited organic growth visibility near term

business.risk: FY27 first-half earnings skew / near-term guidance miss
business.description: Management flagged 1H27 revenue, earnings and EBITA margin will trail the prior corresponding period (defence contract ramp-up costs, QTMP construction-to-manufacturing transition) before a stronger 2H27 recovery — execution risk on this guided skew drove an 11.7% share price fall on the FY26 result
Large individual contracts (e.g., ~$720m Auckland Airport terminal, ~$540m Powerco, ~$500m Chorus) mean loss or delay of a single large program has an outsized earnings impact

financial.description: Net debt/EBITDA improved to 0.8x FY26 (from 2.0x FY23) and BBB rating maintained, but the company still carries hybrid ROADS securities under strategic review, and buyback/dividend increases reduce balance-sheet buffer
Normalised cash conversion of 91-98% in FY25/FY26 has been a key turnaround proof point; working-capital unwind or slower customer payment on ramping defence/rail contracts could pressure this

regulatory.description: ACCC filed civil proceedings in December 2024 against Spotless (Downer subsidiary) alleging cartel conduct with Ventia and BGIS on Defence estate maintenance pricing between 2019-2022; potential penalties and reputational damage with Downer's largest government customer segment

Class action in the Supreme Court of Victoria (since 2023, consolidated from four filings) alleging misleading/deceptive conduct and continuous disclosure breaches tied to the FY20-23 utilities contract misreporting; KPMG (auditor) also joined as a defendant/cross-defendant; outcome and quantum remain uncertain
Heavy reliance on government and quasi-government customers exposes Downer to procurement policy changes, probity reviews and tightening compliance requirements following the 2023 scandal

macro.description: Softness already seen in Australian Transport agency spend and New Zealand discretionary utilities/facilities maintenance spend in FY25; a broader pullback in government capex would compress the order book
Net finance costs (~$82m FY25) affect NPAT; improving leverage reduces sensitivity but higher-for-longer rates raise financing costs on new project debt and working capital
Services/construction model is labour-intensive; wage inflation and skilled-labour shortages in Australia/NZ pressure margins on fixed-price contracts

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Structurally supported by energy transition capex, defence spending growth, and population-driven infrastructure/government services demand in Australia and New Zealand; near-term public transport agency and discretionary utilities maintenance spend has been soft
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — underlying demand for maintenance of essential infrastructure is relatively defensive/non-discretionary, but project/construction revenue and government discretionary spend are more cyclical and tender-timing dependent
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate direct exposure via net finance costs and working capital funding; indirect exposure via government capex appetite
key_input_costs: Steel and construction materials for rail/transport projects

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: underlying NPATA +10% to $306.7m (within $295-315m guidance), statutory NPAT +51% to $225.4m, underlying EBITA +6% to $502.9m, EBITA margin 5.1% (up from 4.4% FY25), cash conversion 91%; pro forma revenue fell ~4.6%; shares fell ~11.7% to $6.58 on FY27 guidance concerns

FY27 guidance flagged a 'larger than normal skew' with 1H27 revenue, earnings and EBITA margin trailing pcp before a stronger 2H27, driven by defence Property & Asset Services contract ramp-up costs and the QTMP transition from construction to manufacturing
Management set FY30 medium-term targets: revenue CAGR 4-5% (FY26-FY30), EBITA margin approaching 6%, average cash conversion >90%

Net debt/EBITDA improved to 0.8x (from 0.9x FY25); dividend reached 29.2cps (100% franked, 31% three-year CAGR); buyback program (~$260m planned) had repurchased ~$96.5m by year end with continuation expected in FY27

Board renewal continued: Teresa Handicott retired as Non-Executive Director at the November 2025 AGM after nine years; Kerry Gleeson (Sep 2025) and Annette Carey (Nov 2025) appointed as new independent Non-Executive Directors

FY25 results: underlying NPATA +33% to $279.4m (top of $265-280m guidance range), underlying EBITA margin 4.4% (vs 3.2% FY24), net debt/EBITDA improved to 0.9x; announced on-market buyback of up to $230m (~5% of issued capital)
Agreement reached (1 July 2025) to sell Downer's 49% interest in Keolis Downer to the Keolis Group, subject to FIRB approval; $38.6m pre-tax impairment taken on the asset held for sale

Completed divestment of non-core Facilities businesses — NZ Catering, Australian Cleaning, NZ Cleaning, and final exit from Australian Laundries (sold remaining 29.9% stake to a Macquarie-run PE fund for a $41.1m gain) — cutting workforce by ~5,000 roles (~40% of Facilities headcount in those units)

ACCC filed civil cartel/price-fixing proceedings against Downer subsidiary Spotless (alongside Ventia and BGIS) relating to Defence estate maintenance pricing conduct in 2019-2022; Downer says it will vigorously defend

Contract wins supporting record work-in-hand: Chorus NZ Field Services Agreement (~$500m/7yr), Powerco NZ Electricity Field Services Agreement (~$540m/12yr), nbn WA fibre upgrade (~$167m), Department of Home Affairs facilities subcontract (~$360m/9yr), Defence CASG package (~$220m/4yr), Ōtaki to North of Levin highway alliance (~$280m)

items.target: Revenue and earnings growth expected for full FY27, but no explicit point range disclosed in available sources
items.notes: Management reaffirmed a positive medium-term outlook for FY27 growth despite a weaker 1H27

items.target: Revenue, earnings and EBITA margin expected to trail the prior corresponding period
items.notes: Described by management as a 'larger than normal skew' to the year, driven by Defence Property & Asset Services contract ramp-up costs and the Queensland Train Manufacturing Program's transition from construction to manufacturing phase; 2H27 expected to be materially stronger
First medium-term (FY30) targets provided at FY26 results

items.vs_prior: raised/extended — builds on FY25's >4.5% average FY25-FY26 LTI target and FY26 actual of 5.1%
items.notes: Incremental improvement path from 5.1% (FY26 actual) toward ~6% by FY30
Consistent with FY25 (98%) and FY26 (91%) actuals, both above the >90% target

items.target: Continuation of on-market buyback program (~$260m total announced) into FY27
items.notes: ~$96.5m repurchased of the program by end FY26; dividend payout target range 60-70% of underlying NPATA

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Peter Tompkins and Chair Mark Menhinnitt characterised FY26 as evidence the turnaround is on-track, with the balance sheet, cost base and portfolio now substantially reset (net debt/EBITDA 0.8x, BBB rating, $38.5bn work-in-hand). Management explicitly flagged 1H27 as softer due to contract ramp-up costs and program transitions, aiming to manage market expectations for a 'larger than normal skew' to the fiscal year, while reaffirming confidence in the medium-term (FY30) targets for revenue growth, margin expansion toward 6%, and sustained high cash conversion. The market's reaction (shares -11.7% on the FY26 result day) suggests skepticism about near-term execution despite the strong trailing results.

bull_case: Multi-year turnaround is delivering: EBITA margin has more than doubled from 2.6% (FY23) to 5.1% (FY26), NPATA has grown for three consecutive years, and net debt/EBITDA has fallen from 2.0x to 0.8x, with cost-out targets consistently beaten

Record $38.5bn work-in-hand (+10% YoY) gives multi-year revenue visibility, underpinned by structural tailwinds in energy transition, defence spending and government infrastructure/services demand in Australia and New Zealand

Capital allocation has shifted decisively to shareholders — buyback restarted and continuing (~$260m program), dividend up to 29.2cps with a 31% three-year CAGR and 100% franking, supported by strong (91-98%) cash conversion
Investment-grade balance sheet (Fitch BBB) and $1.8bn liquidity give flexibility to fund growth and returns without re-leveraging
Management has articulated credible medium-term (FY30) targets — 4-5% revenue CAGR, ~6% EBITA margin, >90% cash conversion — giving investors a roadmap to assess execution against
bear_case: History of governance/risk-control failure is recent and severe: FY23's $539.5m impairment and -$385.7m net loss stemmed from years of undetected contract mispricing, and the consolidated shareholder class action plus ACCC cartel proceedings against Spotless remain unresolved legal overhangs with uncertain financial and reputational consequences

FY27 guidance signals near-term deterioration — management itself flagged 1H27 revenue, earnings and margin will be below the prior year, and the market responded by selling the stock nearly 12% despite a beat-and-raise FY26 result, suggesting limited confidence in the promised 2H27 recovery

Revenue has now declined for three straight years (pro forma) as the company exits contracts — margin-led earnings growth against a shrinking top line is not indefinitely sustainable, and the medium-term 4-5% revenue CAGR target requires a reversal of this trend that has not yet been demonstrated

Structurally thin margins (targeting only ~6% EBITA margin by FY30) in a labour-intensive contracting business leave little buffer against cost inflation, subcontractor risk, or a repeat of prior contract-pricing errors

Heavy dependence on government and government-adjacent customers (Defence, transport agencies, utilities) exposes Downer to procurement policy shifts, budget cycles, and — following the ACCC allegations — potential loss of trust with its largest customer base
